common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: No source gives a tested way to tell the causes apart, or says which is most common (R-1). Sources disagree on sun hours (C-1), on feeding (C-2), on where to cut a blind shoot (C-4), on first-season flowering (C-5), on how hard is too hard (C-6) and on chemical treatment of balling (C-7). Rose midge has no New Zealand or Australian source (R-3). Lower-confidence findings (potassium AF-7, heat AF-9, cold AF-10, hips AF-20, rootstock AF-32, pesticides AF-33) are not used in this answer.

items.text: Pip can't tell you which reason applies to your rose. Here are the reasons sources give, with what to look for and what they suggest.
Too little sun, or too much shade, means fewer flowers.
Sources give a minimum of four to eight hours of direct sun a day. Six is the most common figure.
Trees and shrubs nearby compete with a rose for light, water and food. Sources advise planting roses away from them.
Too much fertiliser, especially nitrogen, gives lots of leafy growth and few flowers.
Too little feeding is also given as a reason, and feeding as a remedy. Pip's care tips give the feeding pattern.
Too little water, or drought, reduces flowering. Sources describe pale, limp leaves, dropped leaves and small flowers.
Pruning too much, too little or at the wrong time is listed as a reason. No source says where too much begins.
Harder pruning gives fewer, larger flowers. Lighter pruning gives more, smaller ones.
Removing spent flowers from a repeat-flowering rose encourages more flowers.

If your rose flowered once in late spring or early summer and not again, it may be a once-flowering variety. Pip can't support those yet. A local rose society or garden centre can help, or you can check its type with Pip's rose-type questions.
Pruning a once-flowering rose before it flowers removes its flowers.
A blind shoot grows and leafs normally but has no flower bud at its tip.
The cause of blind shoots isn't known. Sources suggest weather, shade, over-feeding and big swings between day and night temperatures.
Sources cut a blind shoot back to get a new shoot that can flower. The RHS cuts it back by half to a strong bud. Others cut to the next leaf joint down, or to the next full five-leaflet leaf.
Buds that form but don't open after cool, wet weather may be "balled": the bud feels soft and its outer petals turn brown and papery.
Sources remove balled or rotting buds promptly, and suggest better air flow around the plant and watering at the base, not over the leaves.
Sources link spotted petals with grey fuzz to grey mould (botrytis), which is more common in cool, wet weather.
Sources link brown or white streaks on petals, or distorted flowers, to thrips.
Sources link holes in buds, with caterpillars, to budworm.
Black spot (dark spots on the leaves, then yellowing and leaf drop) weakens a rose so it flowers less.
A photo alone can't show why a rose isn't flowering. Check these signs on the plant itself.
